payload.statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2 and let g be an integer with g >= 0. Define K_{m,g} to be the set of all tuples x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}, and such that x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g. Define K_{m,g+1} analogously with coordinate sum g+1. Then there exists an injective function J_{m,g} from K_{m,g} to K_{m,g+1}.

result_payload.proof_summary: I found a natural existence argument for a coordinate that can be increased by 1 while preserving the defining inequalities: if x\in K_{m,g} is nonempty and t is the smallest index at which x_t attains the global minimum of the coordinates, then increasing x_t by 1 still satisfies all inequalities. The verification is straightforward: inequalities with x_t on the left only become easier; if x_t appears on the right in a non-wrapping relation i+j=t, then i,j<t, so by minimality of t we have x_i,x_j\ge x_t+1, hence x_i+x_j\ge x_t+1; if x_t appears on the right in a wrapping relation i+j-m=t, then x_i,x_j\ge x_t, so x_i+x_j+1\ge x_t+1. However, this does not by itself give an injective map, and the obvious map x\mapsto x+e_t is not injective: for m=3, x=(1,2) and x'=(2,1) both satisfy the defining conditions, and this rule sends both to (2,2). I was unable to repair this into a rigorous injective construction, and I also do not have a counterexample to the existence of some other injective map.

suspected_gaps: I do not have a valid injective construction J_{m,g}.
I cannot prove that the cardinalities |K_{m,g}| are nondecreasing in g from the given self-contained data.
I found a collision for a natural candidate map, so the main missing point is genuinely substantial rather than cosmetic.

result_payload.stuck_point: The key obstruction is injectivity. I can show that every nonempty x in K_{m,g} has at least one coordinate that may be increased by 1 while staying inside K_{m,g+1}, but I could not turn this into a globally injective rule. Natural choices (such as increasing the first or last minimal coordinate) admit explicit collisions.
